title: Tolleson
name: Tolleson
metaDescription: Tolleson 1031 exchange advisory for owners of rail-served warehouse, cold storage, and I-10 distribution buildings in this West Valley industrial city.

sections.html: Tolleson is a small city entirely surrounded by Phoenix, and it built its identity around rail and food distribution long before the rest of the West Valley grew up around it. Union Pacific and BNSF lines still run through town, and produce and cold storage operators have worked out of Tolleson for generations. An owner exchanging out of Tolleson property is trading in one of the Valley's oldest working industrial bases, not a newer suburban market.

sections.heading: Old Rail Freight and New Highway Logistics, Side by Side
sections.html:
Rail-served warehouse and distribution buildings anchor the older parts of Tolleson, many of them still tied to active Union Pacific or BNSF spurs. Food processing and cold storage facilities make up a distinct and long-standing slice of the stock, reflecting the city's history as a produce and distribution hub for the whole Valley. Newer big-box logistics buildings have gone up along the I-10 frontage to serve regional distribution rather than rail freight, and a small legacy retail core downtown still serves the surrounding residential pockets.

Several cold storage buildings in Tolleson trace their operating history back decades under the same family-owned distribution companies, and a change in ownership at the building level doesn't always mean a change in the tenant running the cold chain operation inside it.

sections.heading: What Tends to Show Up on a Tolleson Identification List
sections.html:
Owners exchanging into Tolleson typically consider:

  • Rail-served warehouse and distribution buildings
  • Food processing and cold storage facilities
  • Newer big-box logistics buildings along I-10
  • Legacy retail in the historic downtown core
  • Industrial land near active rail spurs

sections.heading: Confirming Jurisdiction in a City Surrounded by Phoenix
sections.html:
Because Tolleson sits entirely inside Phoenix's boundaries as its own separate city, some parcels near the edges can be easy to mistake for Phoenix jurisdiction when they're actually governed by Tolleson, or the reverse. A buyer should confirm which city holds zoning and permitting authority over a specific parcel before assuming either jurisdiction's rules apply, since the two don't always process approvals the same way.

Utility service can follow a similar split, with some parcels served by Tolleson's own municipal utilities and neighboring parcels served by a Phoenix or private provider, so a buyer should confirm water and sewer provider directly rather than assume service boundaries match the city limits shown on a map.

sections.heading: Rail Access and Refrigeration Infrastructure Need Real Verification
sections.html: A buyer looking at rail-served industrial in Tolleson should confirm directly with Union Pacific or BNSF whether a spur is still active and in what condition, since an abandoned or degraded spur changes a building's value proposition considerably. Cold storage and food processing buildings also carry specialized refrigeration and utility infrastructure that's expensive to replace or reconfigure, so a buyer should get that equipment inspected rather than assume it transfers in usable condition. Given decades of industrial and produce-handling use, a Phase I environmental assessment is a reasonable step on most older Tolleson parcels.

sections.heading: Stable Demand, but Real Competition for the Best Buildings
sections.html: Tolleson's industrial base draws steady demand because of its location and its rail access, and the best rail-served and cold storage buildings can draw competition from institutional logistics buyers working the whole West Valley, well beyond Tolleson itself. An owner should have a broker tracking Tolleson-specific listings well before the relinquished sale closes, since waiting until the identification window opens leaves little room to compete for the stronger buildings. A broker with existing relationships among the cold storage and produce distribution operators can sometimes hear about a building coming available before it's formally listed.

faqs.q: What makes Tolleson different from other West Valley industrial submarkets?
faqs.a: Tolleson's industrial base grew up around rail and food distribution decades before the rest of the West Valley developed, so it has a mix of older rail-served warehouse and cold storage stock alongside newer I-10 logistics buildings, a blend most surrounding submarkets don't offer.

faqs.q: Since Tolleson is surrounded by Phoenix, does Phoenix or Tolleson control zoning there?
faqs.a: It depends on the specific parcel. Confirm which city actually holds zoning and permitting authority before assuming either jurisdiction's rules apply, since boundaries near the edges can be easy to misread and the two cities don't process approvals identically.

faqs.q: How do I know if a rail spur serving a Tolleson building is actually still usable?
faqs.a: Confirm directly with Union Pacific or BNSF rather than relying on the building's marketing materials. An abandoned or degraded spur changes what the property is realistically worth.

faqs.q: Do the same tenants tend to stay in Tolleson's cold storage buildings for a long time?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Several cold storage operations trace back decades under the same family-owned distribution companies, so a change in building ownership doesn't necessarily mean a change in the operating tenant.

faqs.q: Can 1031 Exchange of Phoenix confirm whether my Tolleson purchase qualifies for a 1031 exchange?
faqs.a: No. That determination is made by the investor's qualified intermediary, CPA, or tax attorney. This service coordinates sourcing, timelines, and communication among those advisors, working alongside the investor's own tax counsel.

faqs.q: Does Tolleson provide its own water and sewer service, or does Phoenix handle it?
faqs.a: It varies by parcel. Some properties are served by Tolleson's own municipal utilities while neighboring parcels use a Phoenix or private provider, so confirm the actual service provider rather than assume it matches the city limits on a map, particularly before underwriting utility costs and capacity on an industrial or cold storage building at any given site.
